title: 13  Astronomy
text:
13.4 A note on telescopes
There is a lot to be said for doing observational astronomy with traditional telescopes - the manual handling and the set-up are all part of the hobby. For sheer practicality and getting to the images however It’s hard to beat the new generation of electronic telescopes. Of the field of options, the SeeStar S50 is a clear winner in the features/cost tradeoff. The SeeStar S50 is a compact, smart, all-in-one astronomical imaging telescope that brings modern astrophotography and observation into the classroom or field without the steep learning curve of traditional telescopes.
Unlike conventional telescopes, the SeeStar S50 features automated alignment, tracking, and image stacking, all controlled via an intuitive app interface. This means students spend more time observing and analysing than fiddling with mounts, focus, or celestial coordinates. Its built-in GoTo system lets students select targets—from planets to nebulae—with ease, and the live image stacking produces clearer images over time, demonstrating the real-world application of signal-to-noise ratios and photon detection.
The real pedagogical strength of the S50 lies in its data output and integration possibilities. Students can capture their own high-resolution FITS or JPEG files and analyse them using free astronomy tools like FITS Liberator or AstroImageJ. For more advanced classes, this opens doors to authentic scientific practices—students can measure variable star brightness, investigate the motion of Jupiter’s moons, or even carry out basic spectroscopy using clip-on diffraction gratings or affordable Star Analyser filters. By attaching a simple transmission grating to the front of the aperture or camera, students can record spectra of bright stars or emission lines from planetary nebulae, leading to discussions about atomic transitions, redshift, and the composition of stars.

Astronomy with the SeeStar S50 Smart Telescope

Educational Goals and Learning Outcomes
Students will learn to operate a SeeStar S50 smart telescope to capture real astronomical data. They will plan and image targets (stars, planets, nebulae, Moon, Sun), measure star brightness (photometry), and record basic spectra using a clip-on diffraction grating. By the end of these activities, students will understand how telescope aperture and distance affect brightness (the inverse-square law ), how photon (shot) noise limits measurement precision, and how atomic energy levels produce absorption or emission lines in spectra.
Key skills include using astronomy software for planning and analysis, taking and calibrating images, doing aperture photometry, and identifying spectral lines.


Getting Started: The SeeStar S50
The SeeStar S50 is an all-in-one f/5 50 mm refractor (250 mm focal length) with built-in camera and controller. It includes filters (UV/IR cut, dark, narrowband) and can image deep-sky objects, landscapes, the Sun (with solar filter), or the Moon. The telescope has an ASIAIR-like app interface (SkyAtlas by ZWO) that lets the teacher align and select targets easily. In use, the teacher sets up the tripod and powers the S50; students then use the app to point and focus under supervision.


Power on and align:
Place the S50 on its tripod outdoors. Turn it on and connect your tablet/smartphone to its Wi-Fi. Launch the SkyAtlas app. If needed, do a quick star alignment following on-screen prompts.


Select a target:
Use the built-in database or sky map in the app to pick an object (e.g. Moon, planet, bright star, nebula). The telescope will slews and begins tracking automatically.


Focus and exposure:
Adjust focus via the electronic focuser in the app if stars are fuzzy. Set an appropriate exposure: bright objects (Moon, planets) require <1 s, faint nebulae may need 5–20 s or more. (The S50 will often live-stack images automatically, or you can capture individual frames.) ##### Capture images: Take one or more exposures. Save images in FITS or JPEG format (the S50 records 1920×1080 pixels). FITS is preferred for analysis because it preserves raw data and metadata. The S50’s small aperture collects light over the 50mm area, so distant stars are faint. Remember the inverse-square law: as distance doubles, a star’s brightness falls to one-quarter. For example, a star twice as far away appears 4× dimmer. This law is why very faint stars need long exposures. By comparing images of objects at different distances or brightnesses, students see this law in action.


Solar observations
The safe solar imaging mode lets students study solar rotation or count sunspots. (Never look at the Sun without a proper filter!) These examples illustrate basic observing: students learn to focus, set exposure, and use stacking.


Photometry: Measuring Star Brightness
Photometry is the practice of measuring how bright stars or other objects appear. The steps below guide students through a basic photometry project (e.g. monitoring a variable star’s light curve): Choose a target and comparisons. Select a star of interest (for example, a known variable star or a bright reference star in a cluster). In the same field, identify one or two non-variable comparison stars of similar brightness (check catalogs or Stellarium for magnitudes). Acquire images. With the S50 tracking your target field, take a series of exposures. To reduce noise, it’s common to take many short exposures and combine them. For instance, one experienced observer uses 18 frames of 10s each (total 3min). Save the raw FITS images (turn off on-camera stacking if needed) so you can calibrate and analyze them.

Calibrate images.
(Optional at GCSE level, but good practice.) Take dark frames (same exposure with lens cap on) and bias/flat if possible to correct sensor artifacts. Many S50 users skip complex calibration because the camera output is “calibrated” by default, but at least subtracting darks can improve precision. Load images into analysis software. Free tools like AstroImageJ (AIJ) are ideal. Import the stacked or individual FITS images into AIJ (it can read FITS directly). Configure AIJ for photometry: set plate scale (≈4.87 arcsec/pixel for S50) and select photometry mode.


Perform aperture photometry.
In AIJ, click on the target star and comparison stars to place apertures. The program will sum the pixel counts (signal) within each aperture and subtract background. This yields instrumental magnitudes or fluxes for each star in each image. Compute differential magnitudes. Subtract the target’s magnitude from the comparison star(s) magnitude to get relative brightness. This removes sky transparency and many systematic effects. Plot a light curve. Create a time series of the target’s relative brightness. For a variable star, you should see it vary periodically or in a known pattern. Compare your light curve to published data (for example, AAVSO charts). Photometry connects to physics in several ways. The apparent brightness F of a star follows \(F\propto L/r^2\) (with luminosity \(L\) and distance \(r\)), and astronomers express brightness on a logarithmic magnitude scale. In practice, the S50’s color camera records counts in red, green, blue subpixels. Observers often use only the green channel (called “Tri-G” photometry) as a proxy for the standard Johnson V-band. Because of this, results are approximate magnitudes, but still useful for relative light curves. Another key concept is photon (shot) noise. The noise in counting photons follows Poisson statistics, so the uncertainty in the measured count \(N\) is \(\sqrt{N}\). Thus if you collect \(10{,}000\) photons, the noise is about \(100\) (SNR≈100). Stacking multiple frames increases \(N\) and thus improves SNR (because \(\mathrm{SNR}\approx\sqrt{N}\). In our example of 18×10s frames, stacking yields \(\sim18\) times more signal than a single 10s frame, reducing relative noise. Experienced S50 users report they can reach stars as faint as ~16th magnitude from a suburban sky (Bortle 8) by stacking many exposures. In the quoted example, the observer stacked 18 images and used the green channel (“Tri-G”) to report magnitudes, covering ~6th–16th magnitude stars easily.
From brighter sites, even fainter stars or asteroids can be tracked. This shows the S50 is capable of real scientific photometry when used carefully.
Example student investigation: Measure the light curve of the eclipsing binary Algol. Plan to observe Algol over several hours, capturing images every few minutes. Use at least one nearby steady star as a comparison. Plot Algol’s brightness vs time and identify the characteristic dip during eclipse. Discuss how the measured drop in flux relates to the stars’ relative sizes and orbits.




Basic Spectroscopy with a Diffraction Grating
Spectroscopy spreads starlight into a rainbow of colors, revealing dark absorption lines or bright emission lines. With a simple objective grating (such as a Star Analyzer 100, ~100 lines/mm), the SeeStar S50 can do slitless spectroscopy. Here’s how students can try it:

Attach a grating.
Affix the diffraction grating (e.g. Star Analyzer 100) in front of the S50’s lens. This may require a special filter holder or DIY adapter. The grating should cover the entire aperture. (The teacher should ensure it fits securely.)


Point at a bright target.
Choose a bright star (Vega, Sirius, or even the Moon or Sun). For solar spectra, use the white-light solar filter in front of the grating or an Hα filter and look at an active region. For stars, a single exposure with the bright star will show a zero-order image (un-dispersed star) and the first-order spectrum offset to the side.


Capture the spectrum.
Expose long enough that the first-order spectrum shows a clear rainbow. (For very bright objects, use a shorter exposure.) Save the image (FITS is ideal). The spectrum appears as a line of color; dark absorption bands are visible against the continuum.


Analyze the spectrum.
Using software (e.g. the free VisualSpec or trial RSpec), open the image and select the first-order spectrum. Calibrate wavelengths by identifying known spectral lines (for example, sodium’s doublet at 589nm or hydrogen’s Hα line at 656nm) to set a pixel-to-nanometer scale. Alternatively, measure the pixel separation between known Fraunhofer lines.


Identify elements.
Look for characteristic lines: in stellar spectra, hydrogen Balmer lines (Hα 656.3 nm, Hβ 486.1 nm, Hγ 434.0 nm) often appear. The Sun’s spectrum shows dark Fraunhofer lines (e.g. Hα at 656nm, CaII H and K in violet) where solar atmospheric atoms absorb light. By matching observed lines to reference wavelengths, students can infer which elements are present.
The physics behind this is that atoms absorb (or emit) specific wavelengths corresponding to electron transitions. For example, the hydrogen Balmer series produces visible lines (designated Hα, Hβ, etc.).
Identifying these lines demonstrates quantum energy levels: each line’s wavelength matches a well-known transition in hydrogen, helium, calcium, etc. Example student investigation: After capturing the spectrum of a bright star, have students label at least three absorption lines using a textbook or online spectral atlas. For instance, if the star is of spectral type A (like Vega), its spectrum will show strong hydrogen Balmer lines (A-type stars are hydrogen-rich). Students can verify Hα, Hβ, etc., and discuss how this reveals the star’s classification. They could also observe how a neon or sodium lamp spectrum differs by comparing to reference charts (i.e. identify emission lines from a lamp as a check).


Software and Data Analysis Tools
To plan observations and analyze the data, we recommend these free or low-cost tools: Stellarium (free on PC; mobile paid): A planetarium program to visualize the sky at any time and location. It can help choose targets and their rise/set times. (Advanced users can even configure Stellarium to issue GoTo commands to the telescope via the S50’s ASCOM interface.) SkyAtlas (ZWO app, free): The tablet app used by the S50 for control. Students will use this on-device to take images. AstroImageJ (free): A Java-based image analysis package widely used for differential photometry. It reads FITS images, does aperture photometry, and generates light curves. Useful for the photometry steps above. FITS Liberator (free): A plugin for Photoshop/GIMP or standalone tool to convert FITS files to standard image formats (TIFF/PNG) for viewing or presentation. Students can use this to create colored images from raw data. Siril or Iris (free): Image stacking and processing software. After capturing multiple exposures, Siril can align and combine them to improve faint details (especially useful for deep-sky objects). VisualSpec (free) or RSpec (trial): For spectroscopy, VisualSpec is a free Windows tool to extract and calibrate spectra from images. RSpec is beginner-friendly but requires purchase beyond a 15-day trial. Either tool lets students plot intensity vs. wavelength from their S50 spectra. Astrospheric/Clear Outside/NightShift (free weather apps): Useful for planning observing sessions by checking cloud cover and transparency. Using these tools, students gain experience typical of modern observational astronomy – combining hands-on imaging with software analysis.



Student Investigations and Experiments
To reinforce learning, students can undertake the following projects: ##### Variable star light curves: Choose a known variable (e.g. Algol, Delta Scuti star, or Mira variable) and monitor it over weeks. Measure its changing brightness and determine its period. Compare with published light curves from AAVSO.

Exoplanet transit observation:
to detect the slight dip in brightness when a known exoplanet passes in front of its star (this requires precise photometry and good sky conditions, best done as a class project).


Color-temperature relation:
Image several stars of different spectral types (O, B, A, K, M). Use the color channels or RGB filter wheel to estimate their color indices (e.g. B–V) and relate to temperature.


Inverse-square demonstration:
In class or lab, students could place a lamp and photometer at different distances to verify \(I\propto1/d^2\). While not using the telescope, this cements the concept that distant stars appear dimmer.


Photon noise measurement:
Have students take a series of images of a bright star and measure the star’s flux in each. Plot the mean flux vs. its standard deviation; verify that \(\sigma\approx\sqrt{N}\) as predicted by shot noise.


Spectral classification:
After taking spectra of several stars, students can classify them by comparing their line patterns (e.g. presence/strength of hydrogen lines or Ca H&K lines). Discuss how this relates to stellar temperature and the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.

Lunar/planetary studies:
Use the S50 to image the Moon or planets (e.g. phases of Venus, cloud belts on Jupiter). Students can measure crater sizes in Moon images using the known focal length and pixel scale, relating to geometry.
Each project should include a clear question or hypothesis (e.g. “What is the period of this variable star?”) and use the S50 data to answer it, thereby achieving learning outcomes in data analysis and physics understanding.




Underlying Physics Concepts
Throughout these activities, the following physics principles apply:
Inverse-Square Law: The intensity of light from a source falls off as the square of distance - This explains why faint stars require longer exposures.
Light as Photons: Digital sensors count photons. Because light is quantized, the photon noise (shot noise) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{N}\) (if \(N\) photons are counted). This means that, for example, collecting 4× more photons (e.g. stacking four images) doubles the SNR, since \(SNR \approx \sqrt{N}\).
Optics of a Grating: A transmission diffraction grating disperses light by wavelength according to \(d\sin\theta = m\lambda\) (where \(d\) is grating spacing and \(m\) the order). This spreads the star’s light into a spectrum so that different wavelengths appear at different angles (and thus positions on the image).
Atomic Spectra: Atoms absorb and emit only specific wavelengths. In stellar spectra, absorption lines occur where elements in a star’s atmosphere absorb light. For example, the Fraunhofer lines in the solar spectrum are dark lines caused by such absorption. The hydrogen Balmer lines (Hα, Hβ, etc.) appear as distinct features at 656.3nm, 486.1nm, etc. Identifying these lines in S50 spectra shows students the connection between photon energy and atomic transitions.
Magnitude System: Astronomical brightness is measured in magnitudes, a logarithmic scale: a difference of 1 magnitude corresponds to a factor of ~2.512 in brightness. Students should learn that a star 5 magnitudes fainter is 100× dimmer, and relate the flux measurements (from aperture sums) to relative magnitudes in light curves.
By integrating practical observing with these physics concepts, students gain a deep understanding of how astronomers collect and interpret data.

title: 14  Capacitors
text: 14.1 General theory for this section

title: 14  Capacitors
text:
14.1.1 Definition

Capacitance is the ability of a system to store electric charge per unit potential difference.
A capacitor consists of two conductive plates separated by an insulator (dielectric).

Capacitance is defined as: \[
C = \frac{Q}{V}
\] Where:

\(C\) is capacitance (in farads, F)
\(Q\) is charge stored (in coulombs, C)
\(V\) is potential difference (in volts, V)



14.1.2 Units

\(1 \, \text{F} = 1 \, \text{C/V}\)

Typical capacitors are in \(\mu\)F, nF, or pF due to large unit size.



14.1.3 Energy Stored in a Capacitor
A charged capacitor stores energy in the electric field between the plates:
\[
E = \frac{1}{2} QV = \frac{1}{2} CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}
\]


14.1.4 Capacitance of a Parallel Plate Capacitor
For a parallel plate capacitor:
\[
C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r A}{d}
\]
Where:

\(\varepsilon_0\) = permittivity of free space (\(8.85 \times 10^{-12} \, \text{F/m}\))
\(\varepsilon_r\) = relative permittivity (dimensionless)
\(A\) = area of the plates (m²)
\(d\) = separation between the plates (m)



14.1.5 Combining Capacitors

In Parallel:

Total capacitance adds: \[
    C_{\text{total}} = C_1 + C_2 + \dots
    \]
Same voltage across each capacitor.



In Series:

Reciprocal of total capacitance: \[
\frac{1}{C_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \dots
\]
Same charge on each capacitor.




14.1.6 Charging and Discharging (RC Circuits)
For a capacitor in a circuit with resistance \(R\):

Charging:

Voltage across capacitor: \[
V(t) = V_0 \left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)
\]
Charge: \[
Q(t) = Q_0 \left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)
\]
Current: \[
I(t) = \frac{V_0}{R} e^{-t/RC}
\]



Discharging:

Voltage and charge: \[
V(t) = V_0 e^{-t/RC}, \quad Q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t/RC}
\]
Current: \[
I(t) = -\frac{V_0}{R} e^{-t/RC}
\]




14.1.7 Time Constant

The time constant \(\tau\) is given by: \[
\tau = RC
\]
It represents the time taken for voltage or charge to fall to \(\frac{1}{e} \approx 37\%\) of its initial value.



14.1.8 Applications of Capacitors

Energy storage (e.g. camera flashes)
Timing circuits
Smoothing in power supplies
Filtering in AC circuits

title: 14  Capacitors
text:
14.2 Stories to enritch

14.2.1 The Shocking Leyden Jar (1745) – The First Capacitor
In the 18th century, Pieter van Musschenbroek of Leyden accidentally invented one of the first capacitors: the Leyden jar. He was experimenting with static electricity and stored charge in a glass jar lined with metal foil and filled with water.
When he touched the wire leading into the jar, he received a massive shock — so intense, he wrote that he “would not take a second shock for the kingdom of France.”
This early capacitor could store and release electric charge — and it amazed scientists across Europe. It even became a party trick in salons!


14.2.2 Benjamin Franklin’s Electric Kiss
Ben Franklin, fascinated by Leyden jars, used them in all kinds of experiments. In one infamous case, he proposed a romantic (and dangerous) experiment where a man and a woman stood on insulating blocks and exchanged a charged Leyden jar by kissing.
It worked. The shock delivered through the kiss demonstrated how electric potential builds up and discharges — an early (and painful) demonstration of how capacitors release energy.


14.2.3 The Camera Flash
Have you ever heard the high-pitched whine of an old camera charging before a flash? That sound is the capacitor charging up.
When you press the shutter, the capacitor discharges all its energy in an instant to power the bright flash of light. It’s a perfect example of how capacitors can store energy slowly and release it very quickly — useful in real-world tech.


14.2.4 Supercapacitors in Modern Cars
Modern electric vehicles (like Teslas or buses in China) use supercapacitors to assist with regenerative braking. When the car brakes, kinetic energy is converted into electrical energy and stored instantly in a supercapacitor.
Unlike batteries, which take time to charge and degrade over time, supercapacitors can charge and discharge very quickly and survive millions of cycles.
This technology helps improve energy efficiency and reduce wear on batteries.


14.2.5 Capacitor Failures: The “Capacitor Plague” (2000s)
In the early 2000s, millions of computers and electronics failed due to faulty capacitors made with stolen — but incorrect — electrolyte formulas.
The capacitors would bulge, leak, or explode, taking motherboards and power supplies with them. Entire product lines were ruined, and manufacturers faced massive recalls.
A small component — the humble capacitor — caused a major global electronics scandal.

14.3.2 Capacitor in a camera flash unit
Refer to this as a practical use of capacitors. The energy stored in the capacitor due to the small charging current from the battery over a few tens of seconds is released as one large burst in a fraction of a second.

Age range: 16-18



14.3.3 Timing with a capacitor
Connect a capacitor and a resistor in parallel with a low voltage d.c. supply. Switch on the dc supply and current will flow through the resistor continually but also charge the capacitor. In the supply circuit and the resistor circuit are two thin strips of aluminium foil.
When the one in the supply circuit (1) is broken, the capacitor stops charging, and when the one in the resistor branch (2) is broken the capacitor stops discharging. Therefore the capacitor only discharges in the time between the breaking of the two strips. If this time is short then the current from the capacitor is roughly constant and so Q = It = CAE where AE is the drop in potential across the capacitor. But E = IR and so t = CAE.R/E. Useful for timing a bullet and falling objects as long as t is small. The validity of this could be checked by the pupils. The p.d across the capacitor should be measured with a digital voltmeter with a resistance of some MO.

14.3.4 The smoothing action of a capacitor
A capacitor placed across the output of a rectifier unit will give a smoothing effect to the output. An analogy of this is to use a balloon to smooth the flow of water. Fix a tube to a water tap, and into this fit a T piece with a balloon hanging down from one branch of the T.
As water flows through the tube the balloon will distend. As the flow decreases, the balloon will shrink - maintaining the output flow. If the flow increases the balloon expands, smoothing out the flow, and keeping the flow rate approximately constant. The expansion and contraction of the balloon is analogous to the charging and discharging of the capacitor.

text: 15.1 Basic Theory

title: 15  CurrentElectricity
text:
Electric Charge (\(q\))

Fundamental property of matter causing electric forces.
Measured in Coulombs (C).



Electric Current (\(I\))

Rate of flow of electric charge: \[
I = \frac{Q}{t}
\]
Unit: Ampere (A), where \(1\,A = 1\,C/s\).



Voltage (Potential Difference, \(V\))

Work done per unit charge to move charge between two points: \[
V = \frac{W}{Q}
\]
Unit: Volt (V).



Resistance (\(R\))

Opposition to the flow of electric current.
Ohm’s Law relates voltage, current, and resistance: \[
V = IR
\]
Unit: Ohm (\(\Omega\)).



Ohm’s Law

Current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it (at constant temperature).



Electrical Power (\(P\))

Rate at which electrical energy is transferred: \[
P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
\]
Unit: Watt (W).



Series Circuits

Current is the same through all components: \[
I_{\text{total}} = I_1 = I_2 = \cdots
\]
Total voltage is sum of voltages: \[
V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2 + \cdots
\]
Total resistance: \[
R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots
\]



Parallel Circuits

Voltage is the same across all branches: \[
V_{\text{total}} = V_1 = V_2 = \cdots
\]
Total current is sum of branch currents: \[
I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + \cdots
\]
Total resistance: \[
\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots
\]



Electrical Energy (\(E\))

Energy transferred by current: \[
E = Pt = VI t
\]
Unit: Joule (J).



Conductors and Insulators

Conductors allow free flow of electrons (e.g., metals).
Insulators restrict electron flow (e.g., rubber, glass).

title: 15  CurrentElectricity
text:
15.2 Stories to enritch

15.2.1 Volta and the Frog’s Legs
Topic: Origin of the electric battery Story: Luigi Galvani observed frog legs twitching when touched with metal and concluded it was “animal electricity.” Alessandro Volta disagreed and proved the metals themselves caused the current, leading to the invention of the Voltaic pile—the first true battery. Discussion prompts:

Was Galvani wrong or partially right?
How did Volta’s invention shape the modern world?



15.2.2 The War of the Currents: Edison vs Tesla
Topic: AC vs DC current Story: Edison promoted direct current (DC), while Tesla championed alternating current (AC). Edison launched a campaign to discredit AC, including public animal electrocutions and the invention of the electric chair. Despite this, AC won due to its ability to transmit over long distances. Discussion prompts:

Was Edison ethical?
Why did AC become dominant?



15.2.3 The Tragic Genius of Nikola Tesla
Topic: High voltage, resonance, wireless power Story: Tesla dreamed of delivering free, wireless electricity and built enormous coils to transmit power without wires. He ran out of funding and died alone and impoverished. Yet many of his ideas underpin modern systems like wireless charging and high-frequency electronics. Discussion prompts:

Was Tesla ahead of his time?
How do society and funding affect scientific progress?



15.2.4 Caroline Herschel and Early Batteries
Topic: Scientific instruments and early research Story: Caroline Herschel, one of the first female astronomers, worked with early electrical equipment like Leyden jars. Her meticulous work in astronomy and use of scientific tools broke barriers for women in science. Discussion prompts:

What challenges did women face in early science?
How did electrical devices aid other scientific fields?



15.2.5 The Murder of Georg Ohm’s Reputation
Topic: Ohm’s Law and resistance Story: Georg Ohm discovered the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance (V = IR), but his findings were ridiculed during his lifetime. Only after his death was his law widely accepted and celebrated. Discussion prompts:

Why did the scientific community reject Ohm initially?
What does this reveal about how science progresses?



15.2.6 The Longest Electrical Circuit: Telegraph Wires
Topic: Long-distance current transmission Story: 19th-century telegraph systems used long copper wires stretching across countries. Engineers discovered problems with resistance and signal degradation, leading to developments in materials and circuit design. Discussion prompts:

How do long wires affect current?
What modern problems are similar?



15.2.7 The Accidental Discovery of the Electron
Topic: Cathode rays and current flow Story: J.J. Thomson used a cathode ray tube to discover the electron, proving that atoms contained smaller, negatively charged particles. This work also demonstrated how current is carried in circuits. Discussion prompts:

How does this relate to conventional vs electron flow?
What instruments are based on cathode rays today?



15.2.8 The Electric Chair and Public Perception
Topic: Voltage, danger, ethics Story: As part of his campaign against AC, Edison promoted its use in executions. The first use of the electric chair was horrifyingly botched, but it influenced public perception of electricity’s risks. Discussion prompts:

Can science be used unethically?
How do emotions influence public trust in technology?



15.2.9 The Baghdad Battery?
Topic: Ancient electricity? Story: A 2000-year-old clay jar found near Baghdad may have been an early galvanic cell. Some believe it was used for electroplating; others dismiss the claim. Its purpose remains debated. Discussion prompts:

What counts as scientific evidence?
How would our view of history change if true?



15.2.10 Daniell Cell and the Stable Current
Topic: Reliable sources of EMF Story: The Daniell cell improved on earlier batteries by producing a steady voltage over time. It played a key role in early telegraphy and laid the foundation for practical electric circuits. Discussion prompts:

Why is a steady voltage important in circuits?
What modern technologies rely on this principle?

title: 15  CurrentElectricity
text:
15.3 Practical work and Demos

15.3.1 1. The electron steeplechase!

Repulsion of aluminium strips
Making d.c and a.c visible
Flow of charge
Chicken and a closed circuit
Parallel circuit - the bath analogy
Bulbs in series
A carbon resistor and heat
The transistor switch
Conduction in liquids
The lemon battery
Series circuit puzzle

This analogy is designed to explain energy losses in a series circuit. Imagine that the electrons are running round a steeplechase course. As they go round they lose energy - on the track it would be by going over a barrier, in a circuit it might be by passing through a bulb. When they reach the end of the track, or circuit, they have low energy and must be given a further input of energy - say by a battery - before they can make another circuit.
Two important rules about them - (i) they are not allowed to give up the race - the same number of electrons that leave the start must reach the finish (this emphasises the constancy of current at all points in a series circuit) and (ii) the velocity of the electrons remains unaltered. We assume that they do not lose much, if any, energy on the flat - this is analogous to the low energy loss in the connecting wires of a circuit due to their low resistance.


15.3.2 2. Fusing currents in wires
Find the current at which a wire will fuse, either by a steady increase or by the sudden application of a large current. Wire wool works quite well for this, although a piece of resistance wire stretched between two retort stands glowing bright yellow before it fuses is quite spectacular. For older students a consideration of the radiation emitted by the wire will lead to a study of Stefan’s Law (Energy emitted by a “black body” at absolute temperature T = OAT4 where A is the surface area and is Stefan’s constant). Factors such as the surface area of the wire and the ratio of fusing current to wire diameter could be investigated.

Age range: 11-16 or above for an individual investigation
Apparatus required: •Wire wool •Resistance wire •Ammeter 0 12V dc power supply (8A) ’Heat-resistant mat •Crocodile clips •Leads



15.3.3 3. The human battery
Place one hand on a copper sheet and the other hand on a zinc sheet and measure the potential difference between them. Voltages of about 0.7 V can be produced due to the electrochemical reaction between the two dissimilar metals and the moisture of your hands. As with the lie detector, try the effects of stress on the “volunteer”!

Age range: 14 —18 Apparatus required: •Voltmeter •Zinc sheet ’Copper sheet •Leads •Crocodile clips



15.3.4 4. Surge of current in a light bulb

Investigate the surge of current when a filament light bulb is switched on. It is worth mentioning that switching on is the time when it is most likely that the bulb will blow. The filament has a low resistance when cold, and therefore a large current flows, heating occurs rapidly, there is a large thermal expansion and the resulting thermal shock can break the filament.
The change of resistance of the filament of a bulb with temperature can be seen very easily as an extension to experiment 17. If the supply is adjusted to around 12 V and then switched on, the small bulb lights brilliantly. The current is large, since the 12V 36W bulb is still cold and its resistance is low. As it warms up - this takes a little less than a second - the resistance rises, the current falls and the small bulb’s brightness decreases.


Theory:
Resistance of a metal conductor increases with increasing temperature. As the temperature rises the thermal motion of the atoms within the metal impedes the motion of electrons through it, and so the resistance rises.
Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: 0 12 V bulb in suitable holder •Small torch bulb •12 V power supply



15.3.5 . Hot wire ammeter
Suspend a taut piece of copper wire between two retort stands with its ends fixed to insulated terminals. Hang a 50 g mass from the centre to keep it in tension. Pass a current through it, and measure the depression of the mass. Plot a graph of depression against current. Note that this will work for both a.c and d.c.

Theory:
As a current passes through the wire it will heat up and so expand. The weight hanging from its centre will cause it to sag.
Age range: 13-16
Apparatus required: •Copper wire 28 SWG o Two retort stands, bosses and clamps 0 12V dc supply giving up to 8A •50g mass on metal hanger 0 30 cm ruler in bench clamp o TV camera if possible



15.3.6 6. Birds on high voltage wires
Why is it that birds can sit on high voltage cables without danger? Of course, it is fine if they do not touch the ground or have one foot on the live cable and one on the neutral. When they are standing on a single cable they are quite safe, because the potential difference between their two feet is far too low to be dangerous.

current electricity



15.3.7 7. Conductivity of glass
This is a fascinating demonstration. Take two pieces of thick copper wire, wind one round each end of a soft glass rod, and connect the ends of the wires to a 240V mains power supply in series with a 100 W lamp. Switch on nothing happens, since the glass is an electrical insulator. Now heat the glass strongly with a Bunsen. As the glass becomes molten conduction occurs, and the light comes on.
It is much more impressive with the mains where, once conduction has started, the heat of the current itself is often enough to maintain the current flow. Age range: 14-16 > > Apparatus required: > > •Variac transformer ’Soft glass rod •Bunsen burner •Two lengths of bare copper wire •Wooden clamp ’Crocodile clips •Heat-resistant mat 0 100 W lamp in holder •Three insulated in-line connectors


15.3.8 8. Parallel circuits
Pupils are taught that the addition of a resistor to a circuit will decrease the flow of current and are therefore puzzled when told that two resistors in parallel draw a greater current from the supply than one of the resistors on its own. You can use the traffic analogy to explain this. The addition of a bypass round a town will actually increase the traffic flow on the major road. Similarly, another resistor in parallel with the first will allow more current to flow from the supply. (See also the bath plug analogy shown in experiment 16 on page 211.)


15.3.9 9. Wolf whistling beaver
I have a soft toy beaver bought in France. When you walk in front of it the beaver wolf whistles, but why? In its chest there is a small light sensor, which activates a circuit if the light level changes.
What better way can there be to show the properties of such a sensor?

( oThese used to be available in 2010 from Stock Foille, 16190
Montmoreau, Charente, France. Cost about E15 including postage)



15.3.10 10. Lie detector
This experiment is a fun extension of resistance and simulates a lie detector or embarrassment meter! Wrap pieces of aluminium foil round two toilet rolls, or tape two sheets of foil to the bench.
Connect a 1.5 V cell and a spot galvanometer in series with the foil, and then complete the circuit by getting one of the pupils to hold the toilet rolls. Now try and embarrass them. The conductivity of the skin changes, and as a result the reading on the spot galvanometer changes also. Quite often just sitting there can embarrass the volunteer - they know what secrets about them the rest of the class knows. Resistance between the two hands is of the order of 200 kQ.
Be sensitive here - I never let anyone’s private life get exposed to the others. The same effects occur if the volunteer is put under stress - try asking them some Physics questions!

Demonstration only. Never do this outside school supervision. Only use a 1.5 V cell and never connect it near to a pupil’s head.
Age range: 14-16
Apparatus required: •Two cardboard tubes •Electrical tape •Aluminium foil •Spot galvanometer
•1.5 V cell •Crocodile clips ’Leads



15.3.11 11. Resistance - conducting putty
Use this commercially available material to make different shaped specimens to demonstrate the effect of shape and size on the resistance of a specimen. Even series and parallel circuits can be moulded! Use a couple of metal discs (such as two coins) pressed on to either end of
the specimen as a means of making electrical contact.

Age range: usually 16-18 Apparatus required:
•Conducting putty 0 12V dc power supply •Ammeter and voltmeter •Crocodile clips •Two metal discs •Leads •A high resistance digital ohmmeter can be used instead of the ammeter and voltmeter and power supply



15.3.12 12. Repulsion of aluminium strips
Two slack aluminium strips mounted vertically side by side can be used to show the forces between currents. Make sure that they cannot touch when a current is passed through them. A single folded strip will show 0 the repulsion of currents flowing in opposite directions - down one side and up the other.

Age range: 16-18



15.3.13 13. Making a.c and d.c visible
Take a piece of thick blotting paper, and soak it with some thinly running paste of starch (or flour) mixed with potassium iodide. Allow it to dry, and then mount it on a metal base. Connect the base to one terminal of the supply using a crocodile clip. Run a probe connected to the other terminal of the supply along the paper surface. First use a dc supply and then an ac supply. The dc supply will give a continuous line while the ac will give a series of dashes. The action of the electricity releases iodine ions, which move towards the positive terminal where they react with the starch, giving a dark blue colour.

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Blotting paper •Starch or flour •Probe • Low voltage (12V) Power supply
•Potassium iodide crystals •Crocodile clips •Metal sheet ’Leads



15.3.14 14. Flow of charge
This experiment is designed to measure the drift velocity of ions in a liquid and gives you an idea of the drift velocity of electrons in a piece of metal when a potential difference is filter paper placed across its ends. Soak a rectangle of filter paper in

crvstal

ammonium hydroxide solution, and lay it on a microscope slide. Place an optical pin across each end and clip them in place with crocodile clips.
microscope slide Connect an HT supply with its output current limited to 5 mA across the pins, and place a potassium permanganate crystal in the centre of the paper. Apply a potential difference of 75 crocodile clip V between the crocodile clips and measure the time it takes for the purple colour to travel 1 cm. Doing the whole experiment on a plastic strip with a half millimetre scale marked on it helps, and using a TV camera to view the whole slide on a screen helps even more.

Theory:

In a wire the current is given by the equation I = nAve where v is the drift velocity of the electrons, A the cross sectional area of the wire, n the number of electrons per metre cubed and e the electron charge. Similar values to v can be obtained by this drift velocity experiment. Values of a few mm a minute are common for potential differences of IOOV between electrodes some three or four cm apart.

Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •HT power supply (50-100V) output limited to 5 mA •Crocodile clips •Two optical pins •Microscope slide •Filter paper •Millimetre scale •Stop clock •Potassium permanganate crystals
•Ammonium hydroxide



15.3.15 15. Chicken and a closed circuit
How do you use a toy chicken to show children that you must have a complete circuit for electric current to flow? Hold the chicken in your hand. With any luck it will chirrup, but why? There is a battery in the chicken and in the base there are two contacts. If your hand is slightly moist it completes the circuit.


15.3.16 16. Parallel circuit - the bath analogy
Imagine a bath full of water but with two plugs and plugholes. The
plughole allows water to fall into a tank where a pump pumps it back to the tap. Now turn on the tap and pump, and pull out one of the plugs. Water circulates round - the level of the water in the bath stays the same.
Now pull out the other plug! To keep the water level in the bath the same the pump must work twice as hard the rate of flow of water from the tap is doubled, but the rate of flow of water from the first plughole is unaltered. This is a good analogy with a parallel circuit - the two plugholesPump representing the branches of theworks harder
circuit, the pump replacing the battery, and the tap the wires before they branch. The height of the water in the bath is analogous to the potential in the circuit.


15.3.17 17. Bulbs in series
I always introduce the idea of voltage by comparing the drop in potential round a circuit containing a number of bulbs with the drop in potential energy down a flight of stairs with each stair representing one of the bulbs. From there I go on to show two experiments to demonstrate this.
In the first one connect a 2.5 V torch bulb in series with a 12V 24W bulb. Steadily increase the potential difference across the circuit, and show that initially the small bulb does not blow. They both carry the same current but the greatest potential difference drop occurs across the large bulb.
In the second experiment fifteen 2.5V torch bulbs are connected in series to 40V IA supply. They all light. The same current passes through each - the potential difference drop across each is roughly the same - about 2.5V.

Age range: 13-16
Apparatus required:
•Bulb 12V 24W •Fifteen torch bulbs 2.5V 0.25A •Ammeter 0-1A digital •Leads


A carbon resistor and heat - semiconductor or not?


The effect of raising the temperature of a carbon resistor can be investigated in the following way. Take a 10 MQ resistor, connect it to a high resistance ohmmeter, and mount it in a holder. Use a hair dryer to heat the resistor, and measure the resistance as the temperature changes. The resistance is first seen to fall and then rise again.

Theory: At first the semiconducting nature of carbon is more important - more free electrons are created and the resistance falls. As the temperature gets greater the increased thermal motion gives a greater rise in the resistance - a minimum of resistance is reached, and then it starts to rise.
Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Hair dryer •10 MQ resistor •Mount •High resistance ohmmeter •Leads


15.3.18 19. [The transistor switch]

In a transistor a large collector current is controlled by allowing a very small current to flow through the base of the transistor. Analogies for this could be:


A policeman directing a queue of cars or
an attendant controlling a large queue of people at a football match or (c) a school helper controlling a lunch queue.



Conduction in liquids — the need for ions


This experiment shows that ions are needed for electrical conduction in a liquid.
Set up the circuit as shown in the diagram, and fill the beaker with distilled water. The lack of ions in the water will mean that the bulb does not light.
Now slowly add the salt, stirring all the time. Eventually the bulb will light, and as more salt is added it will become brighter due to the higher concentration of sodium ions and chloride ions in the liquid.

Age range: 11-14
Apparatus required: •Beaker (250 ml will do) •Distilled (deionised) water •Leads •Two crocodile clips •Two pieces of copper to act as electrodes ’Battery or low voltage power supply •Suitable mounted light bulb ’Salt (sodium chloride) •Glass rod as a stirrer


15.3.19 21. The lemon battery
Put two dissimilar metal electrodes (for example copper and zinc) into a lemon. A potential difference of about 1V should be obtained between them. (Lemons usually give about 1.08 V and oranges 0.95 V.) This can either be detected by using a low voltage bulb (more impressive) or a digital voltmeter. I have not really been successful recently with lighting a bulb, but the voltmeter did show that there was something happening.
A way of making this experiment more impressive is to use a set of lemons in series to trickle charge a capacitor. Then discharge this through an LED to give a flash of light like a camera flash.

Age range: 10-18 in slightly different forms
Apparatus required: •Lemons •Electrodes of copper and zinc •Crocodile clips ’Low voltage bulb LED RS 586 447 •Capacitor 220 mF 25 V •dc voltmeter •Leads



15.3.20 22. Series circuit puzzle
Copy and cut out the following pieces and use them to demonstrate the correct connection of components in a series circuit.
You will find that there is only one way in which they will fit together to produce a circuit with the two bulbs and two cells in series.
You could devise a parallel version of this game as well.

Age range: 7-14 Apparatus required: •Card copies of the circuit elements

title: 16  Elasticity
text: 16.1 Basic Theory

title: 16  Elasticity
text:
16.1.1 Stress (\(\sigma\))

Force applied per unit cross-sectional area: \[
\sigma = \frac{F}{A}
\] Where:
\(F\) = applied force (N)
\(A\) = cross-sectional area (m²)
Units: Pascal (Pa)



16.1.2 Strain (\(\varepsilon\))

Measure of deformation (relative change in length): \[
\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}
\] Where:
\(\Delta L\) = change in length (m)
\(L_0\) = original length (m)
Dimensionless (no units)



16.1.3 Young’s Modulus (\(E\))

Ratio of stress to strain in the linear (elastic) region: \[
E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon} = \frac{F/A}{\Delta L / L_0}
\]
Measure of stiffness of the material.
Units: Pascal (Pa)



16.1.4 Hooke’s Law

Within elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain: \[
\sigma \propto \varepsilon \quad \Rightarrow \quad \sigma = E \varepsilon
\]



16.1.5 Elastic Limit and Plastic Deformation

Elastic limit: Maximum stress where material returns to original shape.
Beyond this, plastic deformation occurs (permanent shape change).



16.1.6 Breaking Stress

Stress at which material breaks or fractures.



16.1.7 Elastic Potential Energy

Energy stored in a stretched or compressed material: \[
U = \frac{1}{2} F \Delta L = \frac{1}{2} \sigma \varepsilon V
\] Where:
\(U\) = elastic potential energy (J)
\(V\) = volume of the material (m³)



16.1.8 Stress-Strain Graph

Gradient = Young’s modulus \(E\).
Linear up to elastic limit.
Yield point and fracture point indicate material behavior.



16.1.9 Summary Table









Quantity
Symbol
Formula
Units




Stress
\(\sigma\)
\(\sigma = \frac{F}{A}\)
Pascal (Pa)


Strain
\(\varepsilon\)
\(\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0}\)
Dimensionless


Young’s Modulus
\(E\)
\(E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}\)
Pascal (Pa)


Elastic Potential Energy
\(U\)
\(U = \frac{1}{2} F \Delta L\)
Joule (J)




General theory for this section:
An object obeys Hookels Law if the deformation is directly proportional to the applied force. For example this will apply to a piece of copper wire being stretched by small loads - the actual maximum load depends on the cross sectional area of the wire.
The Young modulus (E) for a material is a measure of how much it will stretch. This is given by the equation E = FL/eA where e is the extension, L the original length, F the applied force and A the cross sectional area of the wire. For steel the Young modulus is 2x 10 11 Pa.

title: 16  Elasticity
text:
16.2 Stories to enritch

16.2.1 Hooke’s Law: The Birth of Elasticity
In 1660, Robert Hooke discovered a simple but powerful relationship: the force needed to stretch a spring is proportional to the extension—now known as Hooke’s Law. His famous phrase, “Ut tensio, sic vis” (“As the extension, so the force”), encapsulates this idea. This discovery laid the foundation for understanding elastic materials.
Reflection: How did a simple spring reveal universal rules about stretching?


16.2.2 The Mystery of Rubber Bands: Why Do They Snap Back?
Rubber behaves differently from metals; it can stretch a lot and still return to shape. Scientists learned this is due to the coiled polymer chains unravelling and recoiling, a concept that challenged classical elasticity theories and bridged physics with chemistry. Rubber’s elasticity is a window into molecular behavior.
Reflection: What’s happening inside rubber when it’s stretched and released?


16.2.3 Galileo’s Early Experiments on Material Stretching
Long before Hooke, Galileo studied how materials deform under load, observing how beams bend and break. His work foreshadowed elasticity concepts and structural engineering principles used today. Galileo connected physics to building safe structures.
Reflection: How did early experiments lead to safer bridges and buildings?


16.2.4 The Elastic Limit and Material Failure
Not all materials stretch forever. Scientists discovered materials have an elastic limit—the maximum stretch after which permanent deformation or breaking occurs. This insight is vital for engineering and safety. Knowing limits keeps structures safe under stress.
Reflection: Why is it important to know how far materials can stretch?


16.2.5 From Steel to Spider Silk: Diverse Elastic Materials
Different materials show a wide range of elastic behaviors—from stiff steel beams to flexible spider silk. Spider silk’s remarkable strength and elasticity inspire new materials science and biomimicry designs. Nature provides blueprints for advanced elastic materials.
Reflection: What can engineers learn from nature’s elastic materials?


16.2.6 The Role of Elasticity in Musical Instruments
Strings and membranes rely on elasticity to produce sound. The tension and stretching of guitar strings, drum skins, or piano wires govern pitch and tone, linking elasticity directly to music. Elasticity creates harmony and rhythm.
Reflection: How does stretching a string change the music it makes?


16.2.7 Elasticity in Sports: The Science Behind Bouncing Balls
Balls, from basketballs to tennis balls, rely on elastic collisions to bounce back after impact. Understanding elasticity helps improve sports equipment design for performance and safety. Elasticity powers the dynamics of play.
Reflection: Why do some balls bounce better than others?


16.2.8 The Discovery of Young’s Modulus
Thomas Young quantified elasticity with a constant measuring stiffness, now called Young’s modulus. It allows comparison of materials by how much they stretch under a given force. Young’s work made elasticity measurable and predictable.
Reflection: How can one number describe how stiff a material is?


16.2.9 Elasticity and Human Biology: Tendons and Muscles
Our bodies use elasticity in tendons and muscles to store and release energy during movement. This natural elasticity enhances efficiency and agility, inspiring prosthetics and robotics. Elasticity is essential for life’s motion.
Reflection: How does elasticity make running and jumping easier?


16.2.10 The History of Stress-Strain Curves
Plotting stress versus strain reveals material behavior under load—elastic, plastic, and breaking points. This tool revolutionized material science and engineering design. Stress-strain curves tell a material’s story.
Reflection: What can a curve reveal about a material’s strength and flexibility?

title: 16  Elasticity
text:
16.3 Practical work and Demos

16.3.1 Uses of elasticity
The following is a list of the applications of elasticity that I have found useful when introducing the topic: A bouncy castle, space hopper, elastic in clothes, bridges, trampolines, trainers, cricket bats, aircraft wings, your muscles, your skin, car bumpers, crash helmets, car and bike suspension and fishing line. Some mountain bikes actually have air suspension forks!


16.3.2 Bending of a beam
As a practical example of bending and shear stresses bend a metre ruler in the laboratory by supporting it at either end and then loading it at its centre. Investigate the effect on the depression of changing both the load and the length of the beam.
A rather nice extension of this uses a filament of glass drawn out from a glass rod, the filament being in the centre of two much fatter end sections. The rod should be held horizontally by its end and then the filament in the centre loaded with masses. A quite surprising deformation can be produced.

All present require eye protection and safety screens should be used. Dispose of the broken glass with care.
Theory:
The depression of the centre of the beam when it is loaded at its centre is proportional to the load and to the length of the beam cubed
Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Slotted masses •String •Metre rule ’Two knife edges on bosses ’Retort stands
•Ruler mounted vertically in base clamp •Glass rod with central filament section •Safety screen ’Goggles



16.3.3 The belly flop
An idea of the very high compressibility modulus of water can be gained from talking about how painful it is to do a “belly flop” into a swimming pool. Itts actually only 100 times worse to launch yourself on to a slab of concrete if the water does not part to let you enter! Bulk modulus of concrete = 100 x10 11 Pa Bulk modulus of water = Pa!

Age range: 16-18



16.3.4 Elasticity of glass
The elastic nature of glass can be seen in old windows. The weight of the glass makes it “creep”, the lower portion of the pane becoming fatter than that above it. Glass is much easier to break when it is scratched - the scratch provides an initial dislocation which then spreads easily when under stress.
Glass fibre may be bent in a circle while a glass block can only suffer small angular deformation before it shatters. This is because of the difference in length between the two sides of the specimen small for the fibre but large for the block for a given angle of deformation.


16.3.5 Energy stored in a rubber band
You may know that if a rubber band is stretched considerably, beyond its elastic limit, it will not return to its original length. This can be shown by adding masses to the lower end of the band and then removing them carefully - recording the corresponding extensions. I have found it better to cut the band into one straight length, giving greater extension for a given mass.

Extension
The non-recoverable energy absorbed by the rubber band may be worked out by finding the area of the hysteresis loop produced by the force-extension graph. It is instructive to calculate the velocity of projection of a paper pellet by a rubber band both with and without allowance for the energy that cannot be recovered. A very rough estimate of the energy stored in a rubber band can be gained by firing a ball upward from a rubber band stretched by a known amount. You should mention the effects of air resistance in both experiments.

Long stretched rubber bands can cause severe eye damage on ‘fly-back’. Eye protection should be used.
Theory:
Non recoverable energy absorbed by the band = Force x Distance = area inside the hysteresis loop
Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Rubber band •Slotted masses •Ruler ’Base clamp to hold the ruler vertical from the floor •Retort stand and clamp •Suitable clamp for holding the rubber band ’Safety spectacles




16.3.6 Shear stress
This can be demonstrated in a number of ways, and it should be pointed out that it is this type of stress that is most likely to be encountered in machines and buildings.

You can show it clearly with a simple pack of playing cards. If the top card is slid sideways while being pressed down on the cards beneath the whole pack will exhibit shear. Don’t use cards that are too slippery!
Make a sausage of plasticine and twist it at one end while holding the other end steady.
Clamp a metre rule to the desk and twist that.
Show how you can rotate your arm - mainly the wrist.


16-18 •Pack of playing cards •Sausage of plasticine ’Ruler ’Arm

Elasticity


16.3.7 Bungee jumping
This can be simulated by using a long piece of elastic and a mass, doing the experiment over a stair well if possible. Elastic bought from a haberdasher’s works well or you might try unraveling a piece of climbing rope. Can you get the length right so that the mass just stops before it hits the ground?
Age range: 14-18 Apparatus required: •Long length of elastic •Masses


16.3.8 Elasticity of rubber when cooled
Many of us will have seen, or heard about, the wonderful demonstrations of the change of elasticity of rubber when cooled in liquid nitrogen. However reasonable results can be obtained by using dry ice (solid carbon dioxide). Try cooling a piece of rubber tube in solid carbon dioxide for a minute or two and then hitting it with a hammer — the rubber shows a marked change in its elasticity and will shatter under the impact. The change in elasticity of a squash ball and a rose petal when put in the solid carbon dioxide is also worth investigating.

Gauntlet style leather gloves and eye protection are needed when handling dry ice (solid carbon dioxide). Safety screens should be used to protect against flying fragments.
Age range: 11-18
Apparatus required: •Squash ball •Rubber tubing ’Flower petal •Hammer •Carbon dioxide cylinder and cloth



16.3.9 Stretching a sock or tights
This experiment relates elasticity to something practical - clothes!
Take some tights - one leg will do - and fix them to a clamp. Load the bottom end with weights and record the force and resulting extension. (Forces of up to 150 N are needed to give a reasonable extension.) Slowly remove the weights and record the extension as they are taken off. Tights are very good; they stretch a lot when loaded and also show a hysteresis effect which apparently disappears when they are washed!!

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: o Tights (one leg will do!) ’Masses •Retort stand, boss and clamp •Ruler



16.3.10 Strength of paper and string
This is an interesting couple of experiments to demonstrate the difference between the shape of a specimen and the way forces are applied to it.

Try and stand a sheet of paper on one end with a 100 g mass on top - the paper collapses. Now roll the paper into a tube - it will easily support the weight of the 100 g.
Hold a piece of string vertically with the 10 g mass tied to the top - let go and the mass falls as the string collapses. Now hold the string from the other end so that the mass is at the bottom - the string easily supports it.


Age range: 11-18 depending on follow up Apparatus required: •Paper 0 100 g and 10 g masses ’String Elasticity



16.3.11 Elasticity of rubber molecules
Stretch a piece of rubber until it becomes difficult. At this point the rubber molecules should have untangled themselves and be aligned along the direction of stress. You will now probably notice that the band looks a little paler and the surface texture may have changed. Now put a pin through the rubber and move the pin about a bit. The rubber will break apart along the line of stretch, which is also along the line of molecules, showing that there is a lower strength between molecular chains than along them.

Age range: 14-18
Apparatus required: •Two clamps •Retort stands etc. •Large slotted masses (up to 5 kg) •Pin •TV camera if possible



16.3.12 Heating in stretched rubber
Put a piece of balloon rubber between your lips and stretch it. As it is stretched you will notice an increase in temperature unlike what happens with a gas - expansion usually means cooling. Alternatively use a rubber band about 1 cm wide. Holding a length of a centimetre or so between your thumbs and forefingers, pull it sharply and then place it quickly against your top lip. The heating effect is very noticeable. Is it that the molecules in the rubber have become more ordered and so they give off heat energy - resulting in a cooling? Blu tack @ works as well.
A strip of rubber cut from a balloon is first stretched and then held against your forehead. This feels warm and when it is allowed to contract it cools down.
Age range: 16-18 Apparatus required: •Rubber balloon •Rubber band o Blu tack @ •Scissors


16.3.13 Whirling springs and Hooke ls Law
Fix a rubber bung to the end of a spring and spin it in either the vertical or horizontal plane. To measure the force you can use a spring balance fixed in the line with a string. Alternatively calculate the value by measuring the radius of orbit and the speed of rotation. Record the reading on a TV camera if possible for slow analysis later.

Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Helical spring •Rubber bung •Ruler •Stop clock •Spring balance •TV camera



16.3.14 Silly putty
This is wonderful stuff and is available in many toyshops so if you see some - buy it! Stocks may not last. There are two different types:
(a) this type glows in the dark especially after being irradiated with ultra violet (b) this type changes colour when it is heated.
Both types have the same elastic properties. If a ball of it is held by one side it will creep (slowly sag), if dropped it will bounce, and if hit with a hammer it will shatter. Another example of the application of a large impulse is if you hold a piece in your hands and then pull it sharply. It will snap — reminiscent of a severe muscle pull !

Eye protection should be worn and a safety screen used to protect against flying fragments. Short wave u.v lamps should only be used where direct radiation is screened from the eye by a sheet of glass or opaque material.
11-18
•Silly putty •Hammer •Ultra violet lamp •Eye protection •Ultra violet goggles

Elasticity


16.3.15 15. Creatures and granite columns - leg strength, height and g

We are made the way we are because of the gravitational pull of our planet. What would the design of other creatures be on planets with widely differing g values? Animals living on planets with very high g values would be expected to have thick legs while those of similar mass that lived on small planets with low g values could be supported by spindly legs!

While we are thinking about creature design, what about considering if animals would black out if they had a long neck and turned round too quickly.
Bone is actually amazingly strong - the compressive breaking stress of solid bone being only about a third that of steel! Pa) A piece of chicken bone can be investigated to show this strength. Eye protection and a safety screen are essential to protect you from flying splinters. The bone is held vertically in a clamp and weights placed on the top of a small platform resting on the bone.

Eye protection and safety screen(s) will be needed to protect all present from flying fragments of bone.

(b) Granite columns
The maximum possible height of a granite column on Earth is around 7800m. Higher than this and it will shatter under its own weight.
Simulate this by a column of damp sand. Put a tin lid on top and load this with masses until the sand column gives way. This should occur at the base. Another way of doing this is to use jelly. Make a tall jelly in a gas jar, measuring cylinder or glass tube. Pour it out vertically and see how much can be outside the support of the tube before it splits apart.

Theory:
Breaking stress = hpg where h is the height of the column and p its density
Age range: 16-18
Apparatus required: •Sand •Water ’Masses o Tin lid ’Chicken bone ’Jelly •Safety goggles and safety screen



16.3.16 Electric strain gauge
A simple model of an electric strain gauge can be made by an arrangement similar to that used for investigating the stretching of fishing line. Take a 2m length of resistance wire (such as nichrome) and clamp one end to the bench. Pass the other end over a pulley and hang a weight on the end. Measure the resistance between two points on the wire as far apart as possible either by using a sensitive ohmmeter or a voltmeter and a microammeter. (Do keep the current low — you do not want any heating effect.) Now increase the load and a change in the resistance of the wire should result. > If pupils do this they should be aware that the wire might get hot enough to burn their skin or ignite paper etc. > > Age range: 16-18 > > Apparatus required: ’Nichrome wire (2m) •Set of weights O G clamp ’Bench pulley ’Ruler > > •Ohmmeter or voltmeter and microammeter

title: 17  Electromagnetism
text: 17.1 Basic Theory

title: 17  Electromagnetism
text:
17.1.1 Electric Current (\(I\))

Flow of electric charge through a conductor.
Defined as charge per unit time: \[
I = \frac{Q}{t}
\]
Unit: Ampere (A), where \(1\,A = 1\,C/s\).



17.1.2 Voltage (Potential Difference, \(V\))

Work done per unit charge to move charge between two points: \[
V = \frac{W}{Q}
\]
Unit: Volt (V).



17.1.3 Resistance (\(R\))

Opposition to current flow in a conductor.
Ohm’s Law relates voltage, current, and resistance: \[
V = IR
\]
Unit: Ohm (\(\Omega\)).



17.1.4 Ohm’s Law

Current through a conductor is proportional to voltage across it, provided temperature is constant.



17.1.5 Magnetic Fields (\(\vec{B}\))

A region where moving charges or magnetic materials experience a force.
Unit: Tesla (T).



17.1.6 Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

A charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) experiences a force: \[
\vec{F} = q \vec{v} \times \vec{B}
\]
Force is perpendicular to both \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\).



17.1.7 Force on a Current-Carrying Wire

A wire of length \(L\) carrying current \(I\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) experiences force: \[
\vec{F} = I \vec{L} \times \vec{B}
\]



17.1.8 Electromagnetic Induction (Faraday’s Law)

A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf (\(\mathcal{E}\)): \[
\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}
\] Where magnetic flux: \[
\Phi_B = \vec{B} \cdot \vec{A} = BA \cos \theta
\]



17.1.9 Lenz’s Law

The induced emf creates a current whose magnetic field opposes the change in flux (negative sign in Faraday’s Law).



17.1.10 Transformers

Use electromagnetic induction to change voltage.
Voltage ratio related to turns ratio: \[
\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}
\] Where:
\(V_p\), \(V_s\) = primary and secondary voltages
\(N_p\), \(N_s\) = number of turns in primary and secondary coils



17.1.11 Maxwell’s Equations (Conceptual Summary)

Describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated and altered by charges and currents.
Predict electromagnetic waves (light).

General theory for this section:
The Greeks discovered magnetism in about 600 BC. They noticed that a substance called lodestone had some strange properties. If a piece of lodestone is hung on a thread it will always point in the same direction. Lodestone - we now call it magnetite - is an oxide of iron, and it was the first known magnetic material. Lodestone will also attract other magnetic materials.
Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The force decreases with increasing separation. Common magnetic materials: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel.
